summary: Colesevelam (Welchol) is a non-absorbed bile acid sequestrant used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to reduce LDL-cholesterol in primary hyperlipidemia (alone or with a statin), to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, and to lower LDL-C in boys and postmenarchal girls 10-17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. The usual adult dose is 6 tablets (3.75 g) once daily or 3 tablets twice daily, or one 3.75 g oral suspension packet daily, always taken with a meal and fluid. It can raise triglycerides and is contraindicated when serum TG exceeds 500 mg/dL or with a history of hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis or bowel obstruction. Because it can reduce the absorption of many co-administered drugs and fat-soluble vitamins, other medications should be taken at least 4 hours before colesevelam.

moa: Colesevelam is a non-absorbed lipid-lowering polymer that binds bile acids in the intestine, impeding their reabsorption. The resulting depletion of the bile acid pool increases hepatic conversion of cholesterol to bile acids, lowering intracellular hepatic cholesterol. This upregulates LDL receptors on hepatocytes, increasing clearance of LDL from the blood and reducing serum LDL-cholesterol. The mechanism by which colesevelam improves glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes is not fully understood.

preg: Colesevelam is not absorbed systemically and is not expected to result in fetal exposure. However, by binding bile acids it may interfere with maternal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; supplementation may be warranted in pregnant women, and the requirements of pregnancy for fat-soluble vitamins should be considered.
lact: Colesevelam is not absorbed systemically by the mother, so breastmilk exposure is not expected. Caution is advised because reduced maternal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins could theoretically affect nutrient content of milk; monitor maternal vitamin status if used long term.
renal: Colesevelam is not absorbed systemically, so no specific dosage adjustment is required in renal impairment.
hepatic: Colesevelam is not absorbed systemically, so no specific dosage adjustment is required in hepatic impairment; standard lipid and triglyceride monitoring still applies.

major: Levothyroxine - reduced absorption; administer levothyroxine at least 4 hours before colesevelam and monitor thyroid function
Phenytoin - reduced phenytoin levels; give phenytoin at least 4 hours before colesevelam and monitor levels
Cyclosporine - decreased cyclosporine exposure; give cyclosporine at least 4 hours before colesevelam and monitor concentrations
moderate: Glyburide - decreased exposure; administer glyburide at least 4 hours before colesevelam
Oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone) - decreased exposure; take oral contraceptive at least 4 hours before colesevelam to preserve efficacy
Warfarin / vitamin K-dependent anticoagulation - reduced fat-soluble vitamin K absorption may alter INR; monitor INR closely

minor: Other co-administered oral drugs - colesevelam may reduce their absorption; separate dosing by 4 hours and monitor effect as needed

interactions.diagnostics: Can increase serum triglyceride concentrations; may reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which can affect related laboratory parameters such as INR in anticoagulated patients.

Take any of your other medicines at least 4 hours before colesevelam, because it can reduce how well they are absorbed
Constipation is common - increase fiber and fluids; tell your doctor if it becomes severe or you have stomach pain or vomiting
Keep up your prescribed diet and exercise; attend blood tests for cholesterol, triglycerides, and (if diabetic) blood sugar

missed: If you miss a dose, take it with your next meal as soon as you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose, and always take it with food and fluid.
overdose: Because colesevelam is not absorbed and is excreted in the feces, systemic toxicity from overdose is unlikely. The chief concern is gastrointestinal: excessive dosing may cause constipation or bowel obstruction. Manage supportively, ensure adequate fluid and fiber intake, and treat constipation or obstruction as clinically indicated.
